item.text: {"question_id":"1B.6","answer":"During 2023, Mexico engaged with proliferation-control mechanisms: it chaired the OAS firearms-trafficking convention’s consultative committee, participated in a Mexico City peer review of Security Council resolution 1540 implementation, and updated its previously submitted 1540 assistance request. Mexico also issued a 2023 statement rejecting weapons of mass destruction and calling for stronger biological-material controls and scrutiny of emerging dual-use technologies. These are attributable to Mexican state representatives or the administration’s official position, but the supplied record does not establish López Obrador’s personal direction, the substance or implementation of the assistance request, domestic licensing or interdiction results, enforcement against firms or factions, or a documented response to detected evasion or assistance. The evidence therefore supports formal engagement and stated policy, with limited proof of effective, ruler-enforced controls.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0020-E003","BATCH-0020-E005","BATCH-0020-E006","BATCH-0043-E004"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0020-E003","BATCH-0020-E005","BATCH-0020-E006","BATCH-0043-E004","BATCH-0053-E004"],"limitations_and_gaps":["No supplied source documents a Mexican domestic licensing, interdiction, prosecution, suspension, or corrective-action case involving proliferation assistance or evasion.","The 1540 assistance request was updated in 2023, but its substance, implementation, and outcome are unspecified.","The peer review and multilateral roles demonstrate engagement, not compliance or effectiveness.","The 2023 statement records official diplomatic positions and calls;
